text.title: Ios Signing And Provisioning Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules every iOS signing and provisioning document MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: The document MUST inventory every signing asset by type with its identifier, expiry date and storage location: each distribution and development certificate, each provisioning profile (bundle ID, type: development / ad-hoc / App Store / enterprise, expiry), each App Store Connect API key (Key ID, Issuer ID, role, where the `.p8` lives), and each APNs key or certificate. An asset without an expiry date or a storage location is incomplete.

rationale.source: Apple Developer documentation: 'Certificates, Identifiers & Profiles'; App Store Connect API 'Creating API Keys'

rule.rationale: The release that fails at 23:50 on submission day fails because a profile nobody listed expired. Every asset has an expiry and a home; the inventory is what turns 'ask the one person who set it up two years ago' into a table someone can act on.

rule.statement: Push notifications MUST use token-based APNs authentication with a `.p8` auth key. Certificate-based APNs auth is allowed only when the document records the constraint that forces it, and then the certificate expiry (one year from issue) MUST appear in the rotation calendar.

rationale.source: Apple Developer documentation: 'Establishing a token-based connection to APNs' and 'Establishing a certificate-based connection to APNs'

rule.rationale: One APNs auth key serves every app on the team and does not expire; an APNs certificate is per app and dies after a year, usually on a weekend. Teams that stay on certificates collect one silent push outage per app per year.

rule.statement: Private key material (`.p12`, `.p8`, certificate private keys) MUST NOT be committed to the app repository or stored in a chat thread or email. The document MUST name the secret store (CI secrets, a fastlane-match style encrypted store, or the team password manager) and the list of people and pipelines with read access. One shared distribution certificate for the team is the default; per-developer distribution certificates are forbidden unless the document explains why.

rationale.source: fastlane match documentation and codesigning guide (docs.fastlane.tools/codesigning); Apple developer account security guidance

rule.rationale: A `.p12` in the repo is a signing identity for anyone who ever cloned it, and rotating it means revoking a certificate that other builds depend on. A single shared certificate in one encrypted store is what makes 'new laptop, ship in ten minutes' possible instead of a day of Xcode signing errors.

rule.statement: Every App Store Connect API key used by CI or tooling MUST be issued with the least role that works (Developer or App Manager; never Admin or Account Holder) and one key per pipeline or vendor so revocation is scoped. Key ID and Issuer ID are recorded in the inventory; the `.p8` is stored at issue time because Apple allows it to be downloaded only once.

rationale.source: Apple Developer documentation: App Store Connect API 'Creating API Keys' (single download of the private key; key roles)

rule.rationale: An Admin key in a CI secret is full control of the account for whoever reads the CI log. And the `.p8` that was 'downloaded to someone's laptop' is gone the day that laptop is, forcing a key rotation across every pipeline that shared it.

rule.statement: Every expiring asset MUST have a rotation entry with a date at least 30 days before expiry and a named person. Distribution certificates and provisioning profiles under the standard Apple Developer Program expire one year after creation; the calendar MUST reflect the actual expiry read from the portal, not an assumed one.

rationale.source: Apple Developer documentation: certificate and provisioning profile validity; widely established release-engineering practice

rule.rationale: A certificate that expires on a Saturday does not fail on Saturday; it fails on the next build, which is the hotfix. Thirty days of lead time turns rotation into a ticket instead of an incident, and a named person turns the ticket into a done ticket.

rule.statement: The document MUST map each build configuration (debug, TestFlight, App Store, enterprise) to its `aps-environment` entitlement value (`development` or `production`) and to the APNs host the backend targets (`api.sandbox.push.apple.com` or `api.push.apple.com`). A build config without this mapping is not release-ready.

rationale.source: Apple Developer documentation: 'aps-environment' entitlement; 'Sending notification requests to APNs' (sandbox and production hosts)

rule.rationale: The classic silent failure: TestFlight builds are signed for production APNs, the backend still points at the sandbox host, and every push returns `BadDeviceToken` while the app looks fine. The mapping table is what lets a reviewer catch it before the marketing campaign does.

rule.statement: For apps built for a client, the app record and bundle ID MUST live under the client's Apple Developer account (its Team ID is recorded), with the agency invited as team members under a named role. Creating the client's app under the agency's account is forbidden; if it already happened, the document MUST include the app-transfer plan.

rationale.source: Apple App Store Connect Help: 'Transfer an app'; widely established practice for outsourced iOS development

rule.rationale: An app under the agency's account becomes a hostage the day the contract ends, and Apple's transfer process has conditions (in-app purchase state, account standing) that can block it for months. Setting ownership right on day one costs one invitation email.

rule.statement: For each certificate type the document MUST state what stops working when it is revoked, verified against Apple's current documentation: which installed builds keep launching, which stop, and which pipelines break. A revocation runbook (who may revoke, what to regenerate, in what order) MUST be present before any key is rotated.

rationale.source: Apple Developer documentation on revoking certificates and provisioning; widely established practice

rule.rationale: The developer who clicks 'revoke and request new certificate' in Xcode to fix a local build has, more than once, killed every ad-hoc and enterprise build in the field. Writing down the blast radius per certificate type is the difference between a five-minute fix and a fleet-wide reinstall.
